reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: A subungual glomus tumour is a small, benign neoplasm arising from the glomus body, a temperature-regulating arteriovenous structure, and typically lodges in the nail bed
The classic triad is paroxysmal severe pain, marked tenderness to point pressure, and pronounced sensitivity to cold
The pain is often disproportionate to the tiny size of the lesion and can be pinpointed to a single spot beneath the nail
A small bluish or reddish discolouration may be visible through the plate, sometimes with a longitudinal ridge or groove
Love's pin test (localised pain on probing) and Hildreth's test (relief of pain with proximal tourniquet ischaemia) support the clinical diagnosis
Magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound help confirm and localise the lesion before surgery
Complete surgical excision is curative and relieves the pain, though incompletely excised or multiple lesions may recur
reference.pathophysiology: A glomus tumour is a benign proliferation of modified smooth-muscle-like glomus cells that normally form part of the glomus body, a specialised arteriovenous shunt involved in thermoregulation and richly supplied with nerve fibres. When such a tumour develops within the confined subungual space, even a very small lesion compresses adjacent tissue and stimulates the abundant local nerves, producing the characteristic paroxysmal pain and cold hypersensitivity. The dense innervation and vascular nature of the tumour explain why pain is provoked by pressure and temperature change and why the discomfort is out of proportion to its size.
additionalDifferentials: Neuroma or other painful nerve tumour
Causalgia or complex regional pain syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Focused clinical tests (Love's pin test, Hildreth's ischaemia test, cold sensitivity)
Magnetic resonance imaging to localise a small subungual lesion
High-resolution ultrasound as an alternative imaging modality
Onychoscopy to identify a bluish or reddish subungual spot and any nail groove
Radiograph to detect any secondary erosion of the underlying phalanx
Histological confirmation of the excised specimen
redFlags: Multiple or recurrent lesions, which may indicate a familial glomangioma syndrome
Atypical, rapidly growing, or infiltrative features suggesting a rare malignant glomus tumour
Bony erosion on imaging requiring careful surgical planning
Persistent pain after excision indicating residual or additional tumour
reference.prognosis: Solitary subungual glomus tumours are benign and surgical excision is typically curative with rapid relief of pain, although incomplete removal or multiple lesions can lead to recurrence and some nail deformity may follow surgery.
pitfalls: Dismissing long-standing localised nail pain as functional and delaying diagnosis for years
Failing to image before surgery, resulting in difficulty locating the tiny lesion
Incomplete excision leading to recurrent symptoms
Overlooking the possibility of multiple lesions in familial cases
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Complete surgical excision of the lesion is curative and typically brings rapid relief of pain
Accurate preoperative localisation with MRI or high-resolution ultrasound to guide a precise, tissue-sparing approach through the nail bed
Ensure complete removal to minimise recurrence, with careful nail bed and plate repair to limit deformity
Interim analgesia and cold avoidance for symptom control before surgery
Histological confirmation of the excised specimen
Follow up for recurrent pain, which usually indicates incomplete excision or a further lesion
